title: The contented served
hook: those who served in contentment and meditated on truth were accepted (Asa di Var, ang 466)

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirbhau: only the Formless is fearless. Today, a pauri about the people who lived close to that One.

Visit a big gurdwara kitchen early in the morning. Someone is stirring a pot of dal the size of a bathtub. Someone is rolling rotis at a speed that looks impossible. An old man is stacking steel plates. Nobody is checking a clock, and nobody is waiting for thanks. Ask one of them why they're there, and they might just shrug and hand you a ball of dough. Guru Nanak described people like this in a single pauri, and it turns on one word.
screen: `A GURDWARA KITCHEN AT DAWN.` → `NOBODY WAITING FOR THANKS.` → `GURU NANAK'S ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: The pauri is on ang 466, and it opens like this, in paraphrase: those who served were the contented ones, the ones who meditated on truth and nothing but truth. The word is santokh. Contentment. You've met it before on this path: Japji calls contentment one of the earrings of the true yogi. Here, it's what makes service real. Then the pauri describes these people. They did not set their foot on the path of wrong. They did good and lived by dharam, by righteousness. They broke the world's chains, and they ate and drank only a little. Then it turns to the One: you are the great giver, always giving more. By greatness, the Great One is found. So why contentment, of all things? Think about what discontent does to service. Serve hoping to be noticed, and every unnoticed hour stings. Serve to get something back, and you're keeping score. Serve while wishing you were somewhere else, and the work feels heavy, and so do you. Contentment takes all of that out. It doesn't mean wanting nothing for the world. It means being at peace with your own share while you work for others. Eating a little is part of the picture: not needing much leaves room for giving. In Sikh life, seva, selfless service, is everywhere: in the langar, in cleaning shoes, in sweeping the floor. This pauri gives seva its inner side. The hands serve. The heart is content. And the pauri says the ones who served that way were accepted.
screen: `SANTOKH: CONTENTMENT.` · `THEY DID GOOD AND ATE LITTLE.` · `DISCONTENT KEEPS SCORE.` · `HANDS SERVE, HEART CONTENT.` · then, large: `THE CONTENTED SERVED.`

segments.voice: Pick one small service you could do soon, washing a few dishes, refilling someone's water, and breathe out any wish to be noticed. Picture yourself doing it fully, finishing, and walking away without needing anyone to see, and feel what that's like in your chest. If you pray, say Waheguru.
Santokh, contentment: Guru Nanak's picture of true servants, content with little through santokh, rooted in truth, doing good without keeping score.
Your line: contented service. The hands serve; the heart is at peace. That's day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara kitchen, cleaning, and serving the community, and this pauri of Asa di Var describes the contented spirit behind it.

chat.says: What makes service real in that pauri? Just working hard?
options: Contentment: the ones who served were at peace with their share, not keeping score.
Hard work alone: the more hours you serve, the more the pauri counts it as real.
Being thanked: service is real once others notice it and honor the one serving.
chat.meaning: Sev keetee santokhee-een: the ones who served were the contented ones. Santokh takes the score-keeping out of seva.
